## Catalog

### Definitions

#### len *(method)*

The number of arguments, positional or named.

```typst
self.len() → int
```

#### at *(method)*

Returns the positional argument at the specified index, or the named argument with the specified name. If the key is an integer, this is equivalent to first calling pos and then array.at. If it is a string, this is equivalent to first calling named and then dictionary.at. Named arguments can also be accessed with field syntax (e.g. arguments(key: 42).key) if no default is needed. Unlike dictionaries, fields on arguments cannot be modified.

```typst
self.at(
```

- `key` — any — Required Positional
  A default value to return if the key is invalid.

#### pos *(method)*

Returns the captured positional arguments as an array.

```typst
self.pos() → array
```

#### named *(method)*

Returns the captured named arguments as a dictionary.

```typst
self.named() → dictionary
```

#### filter

Produces a new arguments with only the arguments for which the value passes the test.

- `test` — function — Required Positional

#### map

A sequence of values. You can construct an array by enclosing a comma-separated sequence of values in parentheses. The values do not have to be of the same type. You can access and update array items with the .at() method. Indices are zero-based and negative indices wrap around to the end of the array. You can iterate over an array using a for loop. Arrays can be added together with the + operator, joined together and multiplied with integers. **Note:** An array of length one needs a trailing comma, as in (1,). This is to disambiguate from a simple parenthesized expressions like (1 + 2) * 3. An empty array is written as ().

```typst
array( bytes array version ) → array
```

- `value` — Required Positional

#### len *(method)*

The number of values in the array.

```typst
self.len() → int
```

#### first

A default value to return if the array is empty.

#### last *(method)*

Returns the last item in the array. May be used on the left-hand side of an assignment. Returns the default value if the array is empty or fails with an error is no default value was specified.

```typst
self.last(default: any ) → any
```

- `default` — any

#### at *(method)*

Returns the item at the specified index in the array. May be used on the left-hand side of an assignment. Returns the default value if the index is out of bounds or fails with an error if no default value was specified.

```typst
self.at(
```

- `index` — any — Required Positional
  A default value to return if the index is out of bounds.

#### push *(method)*

Adds a value to the end of the array.

```typst
self.push( any ) → none
```

- `value` — any — Required Positional

#### pop *(method)*

Removes the last item from the array and returns it. Fails with an error if the array is empty.

```typst
self.pop() → any
```

#### insert

The value to insert into the array.

#### remove *(method)*

Removes the value at the specified index from the array and return it.

```typst
self.remove(
```

- `index` — any — Required Positional
  A default value to return if the index is out of bounds.

#### slice *(method)*

Extracts a subslice of the array. Fails with an error if the start or end index is out of bounds.

```typst
self.slice(
) → array
```

- `start` — int — Required Positional
- `end` — int
  The end index (exclusive). If omitted, the whole slice until the end of the array is extracted. If negative, indexes from the back.

#### contains *(method)*

Whether the array contains the specified value. This method also has dedicated syntax: You can write 2 in (1, 2, 3) instead of (1, 2, 3).contains(2).

```typst
self.contains( any ) → bool
```

- `value` — any — Required Positional

#### find

The function to apply to each item. Must return a boolean.

#### position *(method)*

Searches for an item for which the given function returns true and returns the index of the first match or none if there is no match.

```typst
self.position( function ) → none int
```

- `searcher` — #let values = (1, 7, 4, 6, 9) #values.position(x => calc.even(x))/// Or equivalently: #values.position(calc.even) — Required Positional

#### range

The distance between the generated numbers.

#### filter *(method)*

Default: 1 Produces a new array with only the items from the original one for which the given function returns true.

```typst
self.filter( function ) → array
```

- `test` — function — Required Positional

#### map *(method)*

Produces a new array in which all items from the original one were transformed with the given function.

```typst
self.map( function ) → array
```

- `mapper` — function — Required Positional

#### enumerate

The index returned for the first pair of the returned list. Default: 0

#### zip

The arrays to zip with.

#### fold

Folds all items into a single value using an accumulator function.

```typst
#let array = (1, 2, 3, 4) #array.fold(0, (acc, x) => acc + x)
```

- `init` — function — Required Positional
  The folding function. Must have two parameters: One for the accumulated value and one for an item.

#### sum *(method)*

Sums all items (works for all types that can be added).

```typst
self.sum(default: any ) → any
```

- `default` — any

#### product *(method)*

Calculates the product of all items (works for all types that can be multiplied).

```typst
self.product(default: any ) → any
```

- `default` — any

#### any *(method)*

Whether the given function returns true for any item in the array.

```typst
self.any( function ) → bool
```

- `test` — function — Required Positional

#### all

The function to apply to each item. Must return a boolean.

#### flatten *(method)*

Combine all nested arrays into a single flat one.

```typst
self.flatten() → array
```

#### rev *(method)*

Return a new array with the same items, but in reverse order.

```typst
self.rev() → array
```

#### split

Split the array at occurrences of the specified value.

```typst
#(1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 5).split(2)
```

- `at` — any — Required Positional

#### join *(method)*

Combine all items in the array into one.

```typst
self.join( none any , last: any ,
```

- `separator` — any
  *Positional* Default: none
- `default` — none
  Default: none

#### intersperse

The value that will be placed between each adjacent element.

#### chunks *(method)*

Splits an array into non-overlapping chunks, starting at the beginning, ending with a single remainder chunk. All chunks but the last have chunk-size elements. If exact is set to true, the remainder is dropped if it contains less than chunk-size elements. <table style="width:90%;"> <colgroup>

```typst
self.chunks(
) → array
```

- `chunk-size` — bool — Required Positional
  Whether to discard the remainder if its size is less than chunk-size.

#### windows *(method)*

Returns sliding windows of window-size elements over an array. If the array length is less than window-size, this will return an empty array. Default: false <table style="width:90%;">

```typst
self.windows( int ) → array
```

- `window-size` — int — Required Positional

#### sorted *(method)*

Return a sorted version of this array, optionally by a given key function. The sorting algorithm used is stable. Returns an error if a pair of values selected for comparison could not be compared, or if the key or comparison function (if given) yield an error. To sort according to multiple criteria at once, e.g. in case of equality between some criteria, the key function can return an array. The results are in lexicographic order. <table style="width:90%;">

```typst
self.sorted( key: function , by: function ,
) → array
```

- `key` — #(/"sorted",/"by", "decreasing", "length",
  If given, uses this function to compare every two elements in the array.

#### dedup

Deduplicates all items in the array. Returns a new array with all duplicate items removed. Only the first element of each duplicate is kept.

```typst
#(3, 3, 1, 2, 3).dedup()
```

- `key` — #("apple", "banana", " apple ").dedup(key: s => s.trim())

#### reduce

Reduces the elements to a single one, by repeatedly applying a reducing operation. If the array is empty, returns none, otherwise, returns the result of the reduction. The reducing function is a closure with two arguments: an “accumulator”, and an element. For arrays with at least one element, this is the same as array.fold with the first element of the array as the initial accumulator value, folding every subsequent element into it.

```typst
#let array = (2, 1, 4, 3) #array.reduce((acc, x) => calc.max(acc, x))
```

- `reducer` — function — Required Positional

### 3.5.3 assert

#### assert.eq

Ensures that two values are equal. Fails with an error if the first value is not equal to the second. Does not produce any output in the document.

```typst
#assert.eq(10, 10)
```

- `left` — str — Required Positional
  The second value to compare.

#### ne

3.5.3 assert

```typst
#bytes("Hello 😃") \ #bytes((123, 160, 22, 0))
```

- `left` — str — Required Positional
  The second value to compare.
- `value` — Required Positional

#### len *(method)*

The length in bytes.

```typst
self.len() → int
```

#### at

Returns the byte at the specified index. Returns the default value if the index is out of bounds or fails with an error if no default value was specified.

- `index` — any — Required Positional
  A default value to return if the index is out of bounds.

#### slice *(method)*

Extracts a subslice of the bytes. Fails with an error if the start or end index is out of bounds.

```typst
self.slice(
) → bytes
```

- `start` — int — Required Positional
- `end` — int
  The end index (exclusive). If omitted, the whole slice until the end is extracted.

### 3.5.7 Calculation (module `calc`)

#### calc.abs

Calculates the absolute value of a numeric value.

```typst
#calc.abs(-5) \ #calc.abs(5pt - 2cm) \ #calc.abs(2fr) \
#calc.abs(decimal("-342.440"))
```

- `value` — int — Required Positional

#### calc.pow

Raises a value to some exponent.

```typst
#calc.pow(2, 3) \
#calc.pow(decimal("2.5"), 2)
```

- `base` — int — Required Positional
  If this is a decimal, the exponent can only be an integer.
- `exponent` — float
  The exponent of the power.

#### calc.exp

Raises a value to some exponent of 𝑒.

```typst
#calc.exp(1)
```

- `exponent` — int — Required Positional

#### calc.sqrt

Calculates the square root of a number.

```typst
#calc.sqrt(16) \ #calc.sqrt(2.5)
```

- `value` — int — Required Positional

#### calc.root

Calculates the real 𝑛th root of a number. If the number is negative, then 𝑛 must be odd.

```typst
#calc.root(16.0, 4) \
#calc.root(27.0, 3)
```

- `radicand` — int — Required Positional
  The value of 𝑛.

#### calc.sin

Calculates the sine of an angle. When called with an integer or a float, they will be interpreted as radians.

```typst
#calc.sin(1.5) \ #calc.sin(90deg)
```

- `angle` — int — Required Positional

#### calc.cos

Calculates the cosine of an angle. When called with an integer or a float, they will be interpreted as radians.

```typst
calc.cos( int float angle ) → float
```

- `angle` — int — Required Positional

#### calc.tan

Calculates the tangent of an angle. When called with an integer or a float, they will be interpreted as radians.

```typst
#calc.tan(1.5) \ #calc.tan(90deg)
```

- `angle` — int — Required Positional

#### calc.asin

The number whose arccosine to calculate. Must be between −1 and 1. Calculates the arctangent of a number.

```typst
calc.atan( int float ) → angle
```

- `value` — int — Required Positional

#### calc.atan2

The 𝑦 coordinate.

#### calc.sinh

Calculates the hyperbolic sine of a hyperbolic angle. The hyperbolic sine of 𝑥 is defined as follows: 𝑒𝑥 − 𝑒−𝑥

```typst
calc.sinh( float ) → float
```

- `value` — float — Required Positional

#### calc.cosh

Calculates the hyperbolic cosine of a hyperbolic angle. The hyperbolic cosine of 𝑥 is defined as follows:


#### calc.value

A map from string keys to values. You can construct a dictionary by enclosing comma-separated key: value pairs in parentheses. The values do not have to be of the same type. Since empty parentheses already yield an empty array, you have to use the special (:) syntax to create an empty dictionary. A dictionary is conceptually similar to an array, but it is indexed by strings instead of integers. You can access and create dictionary entries with the .at() method. If you know the key statically, you can alternatively use field access notation (.key) to access the value. To check whether a key is present in the dictionary, use the in keyword. You can iterate over the pairs in a dictionary using a for loop. This will iterate in the order the pairs were inserted / declared initially.

```typst
#dictionary(sys).at("version")
```

### 3.5.20 panic

#### The project root

Make sure that the main file is contained in the folder’s subtree, so that Typst can access it. In the web app, the project itself is the root directory. You can always read all files within it, no matter which one is previewed (via the eye toggle next to each Typst file in the file panel).

#### Package roots

Just like the project, each package you import has its own root. Within a package, absolute paths point to the package root rather than the project root. On its own, code in a package cannot construct a path that lives in the project or another package. If you need to provide a package with resources from the project (such as a logo image), you can do so by explicitly creating a path to the resource in your code with the path constructor. You can then pass the resulting path to the package. An example of this is shown in the section “The path type”3.5.21/2 above. Alternatively, you can perform the path operation in your code and pass the result to the package. This could, for example, be the result of a read call or a complete image (e.g. as a named parameter logo: image("mylogo.svg")). Note that if you pass an image to a package like this, you can still customize the image’s appearance with a set rule within the package. For now, the path type’s purpose is limited to correctly handling and transferring paths across files in your project and packages. In the future, it may enable additional capabilities like checking for the existence of a file or enumerating files in a directory.

```typst
// A relative path without a leading slash.
// May optionally start with `./`. #path("relative/path/to/file.typ") #path("./relative/path/to/file.typ")
// An absolute path with a leading slash. #path("/absolute/path/to/file.typ")
```

#### path

- If the path is absolute, it is resolved relative to the root of the project or package in which this function is called. - If the path is relative, it is resolved relative to the file where this function is called. If this is already a path, it is returned unchanged.

### 3.5.22 plugin

#### Exports

A plugin module can export functions to make them callable from Typst. To conform to the protocol, an exported function should: - Take n 32-bit integer arguments a_1, a_2, …, a_n (interpreted as lengths, so usize/size_t may be preferable), and return one 32-bit integer. - The function should first allocate a buffer buf of length a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_n, and then call wasm_minimal_protocol_write_args_to_buffer(buf.ptr).

#### Imports

Plugin modules need to import two functions that are provided by the runtime. (Types and functions are described using WAT syntax.) - (import "typst_env" "wasm_minimal_protocol_write_args_to_buffer" (func (param i32))) Writes the arguments for the current function into a plugin-allocated buffer. When a plugin function is called, it receives the lengths.1 of its input buffers as arguments. It should then allocate a buffer whose capacity is at least the sum of these lengths. It should then call this function with a ptr to the buffer to fill it with the arguments, one after another. - (import "typst_env" "wasm_minimal_protocol_send_result_to_host" (func (param i32 i32)))

```typst
plugin( str path bytes ) → module
```

#### source

[B]<https://github.com/typst-community/wasm-minimal-protocol/tree/main/crates/wasi-stub> [C]<https://github.com/typst-community/wasm-minimal-protocol> 3.5.22 plugin

#### transition

Calls a plugin function that has side effects and returns a new module with plugin functions that are guaranteed to have observed the results of the mutable call. Note that calling an impure function through a normal function call (without use of the transition API) is forbidden and leads to unpredictable behaviour. Read the section on purity for more details. In the example below, we load the plugin hello-mut.wasm which exports two functions: The get() function retrieves a global array as a string. The add(value) function adds a value to the global array. We call add via the transition API. The call mutated.get() on the derived module will observe the addition. Meanwhile the original module remains untouched as demonstrated by the base.get() call.

```typst
regex( str ) → regex
```

- `func` — regex — Required Positional
  The byte buffers to call the function with.
- `regex` — str — Required Positional
  Both Typst strings and regular expressions use backslashes for escaping. To produce a regex escape sequence that is also valid in Typst, you need to escape the backslash itself (e.g., writing regex("
- `or` — Variadic
- `and` — Variadic

Splits a string at matches of a specified pattern and returns an array of the resulting parts. When the empty string is used as a separator, it separates every character (i.e., Unicode code point) in the string, along with the beginning and end of the string. ### Definitions

#### bibliography

A bibliography / reference listing. You can create a new bibliography by calling this function with a path to a bibliography file in either one of two formats: - A Hayagriva .yaml/.yml file. Hayagriva is a new bibliography file format designed for use with Typst. Visit its documentation[A] for more details.

### Fields Typical Styles

#### sources

- A path string or path to load a bibliography file from. - Raw bytes from which the bibliography should be decoded. - An array where each item is one of the above.

#### title

Whether to include all works from the given bibliography files, even those that weren’t cited in the document. To selectively add individual cited works without showing them, you can also use the cite function with form.3 set to none.

#### style

This can be: - A string with the name of one of the built-in styles (see below). Some of the styles listed below appear twice, once with their full name and once with a short alias. - A path string or path to a CSL file[A]. - Raw bytes from which a CSL style should be decoded.

### Variant Details

#### target

Typst will automatically assign each citation in the document to a bibliography. Concretely, a citation will be assigned to (in order of precedence) 1. the first bibliography that includes it in its target selector; or if no such bibliography exists 2. the closest *following* bibliography with target: auto that contains its key; or if no such bibliography follows 3. the closest *preceding* bibliography with target: auto that contains its key.

```typst
#let info(body) = block( stroke: (left: 1.5pt + blue), fill: aqua.lighten(50%), inset: 1em,
bibliography( "works.bib", title: none,
#info[
#bibliography("works.bib")
```

#### Format-specific considerations

Metadata is embedded into the output to varying extents: - PDF export supports the full range of metadata and emits it into the PDF *document information dictionary* as well as XMP metadata. - HTML export only supports the title, description, author, and keywords properties. The date property is not supported as the HTML standard has no provision for it.

```typst
#document("list.html", title: [My Famous List])[ #title()
```

#### Metadata

Note that document set rules within a document override explicit arguments passed to the document element. Moreover, properties configured as explicit arguments to document are made contextually available:

- `format` — Settable; default: auto
  Which format to export in. If auto, Typst attempts to infer the export format from the path’s.1 file extension. This property is only supported in the bundle target.

#### title

By default, the configured title is not visibly rendered in the document. You can add the title to the document’s contents by using the title element. It will automatically pick up the title configured here. Adding a title is important for accessibility, as it makes it easier to navigate to your document and identify it among other open documents. When exporting to PDF/UA, a title is required.

#### alt

When you add an alternative description, AT will read both it and the caption (if any). However, the content of the figure itself will be skipped. When the body of your figure is an imag e with its own alt text set, this parameter should not be used on the figure element. Likewise, do not use this parameter when the figure contains a table, code, or other content that is already accessible. In such cases, the content of the figure will be read by AT, and adding an alternative description would lead to a loss of information. You can learn how to write good alternative descriptions in the Accessibility Guide.

By default, this is set to end, which aligns enum numbers horizontally towards the end of the current text direction (in a left-to-right script, for example, this is the same as right). The choice of end for horizontal alignment of enum numbers is usually preferred over start, as numbers then grow away from the text instead of towards it. #### leading

The spacing between lines. Leading defines the spacing between the bottom edg e.15 of one line and the top edg e.14 of the following line. By default, these two properties are up to the font, but they can also be configured manually with a text set rule. By setting top edge, bottom edge, and leading, you can also configure a consistent baseline-to-baseline distance. You could, for instance, set the leading to 1em, the top-edge to 0.8em, and the bottom-edge to -0.2em to get a baseline gap of exactly 2em. The exact distribution of the top- and bottom-edge values affects the bounds of the first and last line.

#### spacing

The spacing between paragraphs. Just like leading, this defines the spacing between the bottom edge of a paragraph’s last line and the top edge of the next paragraph’s first line. Spacing acts both above and below, collapsing to the greater of the amounts defined by adjacent paragraphs. When a paragraph is adjacent to a block, that block’s above or below property takes precedence over the paragraph spacing. Headings, for instance, reduce the spacing below them by default for a better look.

#### justify

Whether to justify text in its line. Hyphenation will be enabled for justified paragraphs if the text function’s hyphenate property.20 is set to auto and the current language is known. Note that the current alignment.1 still has an effect on the placement of the last line except if it ends with a justified line break.1. By default, Typst only changes the spacing between words to achieve justification. However, you can also al-low it to adjust the spacing between individual characters using the justification-limits property.4.

This lets Typst search through all available fonts for the most similar one that has the necessary glyphs. *Note:* Currently, there are no warnings when fallback is disabled and no glyphs are found. Since most fonts are only available either in an italic or oblique style, the difference between italic and oblique style is rarely observable. #### ligatures

Whether standard ligatures are active. Certain letter combinations like “fi” are often displayed as a single merged glyph called a *ligature.* Setting this to false disables these ligatures by turning off the OpenType liga and clig font features. Note that some programming fonts use other OpenType font features to implement “ligatures,” including the contextual alternates (calt) feature, which is also enabled by default. #### scr

There are two ways that fonts can support differentiating cal and scr. The first is using Unicode variation sequences. This works out of the box in Typst, however only a few math fonts currently support this. The other way is using font features.32. For example, the roundhand style might be available in a font through the *stylistic set.24 1* (ss01) feature. To use it in Typst, you could then define your own version of scr like in the example below. Example · Recreation using stylistic set 1

```typst
#let scr(it) = text( stylistic-set: 1,
```

#### height

Whether the page is flipped into landscape orientation.

```typst

#set align(bottom + end) #text(14pt)[*Sam H. Richards*] \

```

#### margin

- auto: The margins are set automatically to 2.5/21 times the smaller dimension of the page. This results in 2.5 cm margins for an A4 page. - A single length: The same margin on all sides. - A dictionary: With a dictionary, the margins can be set individually. The dictionary can contain the following keys in order of precedence: - top: The top margin.

```typst
#set page( width: 3cm, height: 4cm,
#rect(
```

#### bleed

The bleed is the area of content that extends beyond the final trimmed size of the page. It ensures that no unprinted edges appear in the final product, even if minor trimming misalignments occur. Accepted values: - A single length: The same bleed on all sides. - A dictionary: With a dictionary, the bleed margins can be set individually. The dictionary may include the following keys, listed in order of precedence:

```typst
#set page( width: 8cm, height: 5cm, margin: 1cm,
// The bleed is not visible in the preview;
// it exceeds beyond the page. bleed: 0.5cm,
// Fills the entire bleed area, so there will
// be no white strips after printing and trimming. background: rect(width: 100%, height: 100%, fill: aqua),
#rect(width: 100%, height: 100%, fill: white)
```

#### binding

How many columns the page has. If you need to insert columns into a page or other container, you can also use the columns function. <table style="width:91%;"> <colgroup>

#### fill

Setting this to something non-transparent instructs the printer to color the complete page. If you are considering larger production runs, it may be more environmentally friendly and cost-effective to source pre-dyed pages and not set this property. When set to none, the background becomes transparent. Note that PDF pages will still appear with a (usually white) background in viewers, but they are actually transparent. (If you print them, no color is used for the background.) The default of auto results in none for PDF output, and white for PNG and SVG.

```typst
#set page(fill: rgb("444352")) #set text(fill: rgb("fdfdfd"))
```

#### numbering

1. The first number is the current page number. 2. The second number is the total number of pages. In a numbering pattern, the second number can be omitted. If a function is passed, it will receive one argument in the context of links or references, and two arguments when producing the visible page numbers. These are logical numbers controlled by the page counter, and may thus not match the physical numbers. Specifically, they are the current.1 and the final.4 value of counter(page). See the counter documentation for more details. If an explicit footer (or header for top-aligned.12 numbering) is given, the numbering is ignored.

```typst
#set page( height: 100pt,
#lorem(48)
```

#### supplement

The alignment of the page numbering. If the vertical component is top, the numbering is placed into the header and if it is bottom, it is placed in the footer. Horizon alignment is forbidden. If an explicit matching header or footer is given, the numbering is ignored. <table style="width:90%;"> <colgroup>

The amount the header is raised into the top margin. Ratios are relative to the height of the top margin.

#### footer

The amount the footer is lowered into the bottom margin. Ratios are relative to the height of the bottom margin.

If true, the spacing collapses at the start or end of a paragraph. Moreover, from multiple adjacent weak spacings all but the largest one collapse. ### Variant Details

#### radial

Creates a new radial gradient, in which colors radiate away from an origin. The gradient is defined by two circles: the focal circle and the end circle. The focal circle is a circle with center focal-center and radius focal-radius, that defines the points at which the gradient starts and has the color of the first stop. The end circle is a circle with center center and radius radius, that defines the points at which the gradient ends and has the color of the last stop. The gradient is then interpolated between these two circles. Using these four values, also called the focal point for the starting circle and the center and radius for the end circle, we can define a gradient with more interesting properties than a basic radial gradient.

```typst
#stack( dir: ltr,
circle(fill: gradient.radial(
circle(fill: gradient.radial(
```

- `stops` — color — Required Positional Variadic
- `space` — str
  Default: auto
- `relative` — auto
  Default: auto

#### conic

Creates a new conic gradient, in which colors change radially around a center point. You can control the center point of the gradient by using the center argument. By default, the center point is the center of the shape.

```typst
#stack( dir: ltr,
circle(fill: gradient.conic(
circle(fill: gradient.conic(
```

- `stops` — any — Required Positional Variadic
  Default: 0deg
- `space` — spot
  Default: auto
- `relative` — auto
  Default: auto

#### sharp

Creates a sharp version of this gradient. Sharp gradients have discrete jumps between colors, instead of a smooth transition. They are particularly useful for creating color lists for a preset gradient.

```typst

#rect(fill: grad.sharp(5))
#rect(fill: grad.sharp(5, smoothness: 20%))
```

  How much to smooth the gradient.

#### source

By default, the format is detected automatically. Typically, you thus only need to specify this when providing raw bytes as the source (even then, Typst will try to figure out the format automatically, but that’s not always possible). Supported formats are "png", "jpg", "gif", "svg", "pdf", "webp" as well as raw pixel data. Note that several restrictions apply when using PDF files as images: - When exporting to PDF, any PDF image file used must have a version equal to or lower than the export target PDF version. - PDF files as images are currently not supported when exporting with a specific PDF standard, like PDF/ A-3 or PDF/UA-1. In these cases, you can instead use SVGs to embed vector images.


#### miter-limit

A repeating tiling fill. Typst supports the most common type of tilings, where a pattern is repeated in a grid-like fashion, covering the entire area of an element that is filled or stroked. The pattern is defined by a tile size and a body defining the content of each cell. You can also add horizontal or vertical spacing between the cells of the tiling and offset the starting position of the tiling.

```typst
tiling(
) → tiling
```

#### size

Shifts the entire tile grid without affecting the tile size or spacing. Default: (0% + 0pt, 0% + 0pt) The offset is specified as a (x, y) pair. Positive x values move the pattern to the right and positive y values move it down. Relative values are resolved against the tile size plus spacing.

```typst
#set rect(width: 100%, height: 80pt, stroke: 1pt)
#let pat = tiling( size: (20pt, 20pt),
circle(radius: 10pt, fill: blue),
#let pat-with-offset = tiling( size: (20pt, 20pt),
#grid(
rect(fill: pat-with-offset),
```

#### relative

The content of each cell of the tiling.

- `key`
  - If it is a string, creates a custom counter that is only affected by manual updates, - If it is the page function, counts through pages, - If it is a selector, counts through elements that match the

### Definitions

#### get Contextual *(method)*

Retrieves the value of the counter at the current location. Always returns an array of integers, even if the counter has just one number. This is equivalent to counter.at(here()).

```typst
self.get() → int array
```

#### display Contextual *(method)*

Displays the value of the counter. You can provide both a custom numbering and a custom location. Both default to auto, selecting sensible defaults (the numbering of the counted element and the current location, respectively). Returns the formatted output.

```typst
self.display(
```

- `numbering` — function
  *Positional* Default: auto
- `at` — bool
  Default: auto

#### at Contextual *(method)*

Retrieves the value of the counter at the given location. Always returns an array of integers, even if the counter has just one number. The selector must match exactly one element in the document. The most useful kinds of selectors for this are labels and locations.

```typst
self.at( label selector location function ) → int array
```

- `selector` — label — Required Positional

#### final Contextual *(method)*

Retrieves the value of the counter at the end of the document. Always returns an array of integers, even if the counter has just one number.

```typst
self.final() → int array
```

#### step

The depth at which to step the counter. Defaults to 1.

#### update *(method)*

Updates the value of the counter. Just like with step, the update only occurs if you put the resulting content into the document. Default: 1

```typst
self.update( int array function ) → content
```

- `update` — int — Required Positional

### 3.12.3 locate Contextual

#### selector

Identifies an element in the document. A location uniquely identifies an element in the document and lets you access its absolute position on the pages. You can retrieve the current location with the here function and the location of a queried or shown element with the location() method on content. Elements that are automatically assigned a location are called *locatable.* For efficiency reasons, not all elements are locatable. - In the Model categ ory, most elements are locatable. This is because semantic elements like heading s and figures are often used with introspection.

#### page

Returns the page number for this location. Note that this does not return the value of the pag e counter at this location, but the true page number (starting from one).

```typst
#context [
```

#### position *(method)*

Returns a dictionary with the page number and the x, y position for this location. The page number starts at one and the coordinates are measured from the top-left of the page. If you only need the page number, use page() instead as it allows Typst to skip unnecessary work.

```typst
self.position() → dictionary
```

#### page-numbering

Returns the page numbering pattern of the page at this location. This can be used when displaying the page counter in order to obtain the local numbering. This is useful if you are building custom indices or outlines. If the page numbering is set to none at that location, this function returns none.

```typst
state(
) → state
```

- `key` — #let banana = state("key", "🍌") #let broccoli = state("key", "🥦")/#banana.update(it => it + "😋") #context [/- #state("key", "🍎").get() — Required Positional
  Any updates.4 to the state will be identified with the string key. If you construct multiple states with the same key, then updating any one will affect all of them.

#### metadata

Exposes a value to the query system without producing visible content. This element can be retrieved with the query function and from the command line with typst query. Its purpose is to expose an arbitrary value to the introspection system. To identify a metadata value among others, you can attach a label to it and query for that label. The metadata element is especially useful for command line queries because it allows you to expose arbitrary values to the outside world.

#### get Contextual *(method)*

```typst
self.get() → any
```

#### at Contextual *(method)*

Retrieves the value of the state at the given selector’s unique match. The selector must match exactly one element in the document. The most useful kinds of selectors for this are labels and locations.

```typst
self.at( label selector location function ) → any
```

- `selector` — label — Required Positional

#### final Contextual *(method)*

Retrieves the value of the state at the end of the document.

```typst
self.final() → any
```

#### update *(method)*

Updates the value of the state. Returns an invisible piece of content that must be inserted into the document to take effect. This invisible content tells Typst that the specified update should take place wherever the content is inserted into the document. State is a part of your document and runs like a thread embedded in the document content. The value of a state is the result of all state updates that happened in the document up until that point. That’s why state.update returns an invisible sliver of content that you need to return and include in the document — a state update that is not “placed” in the document does not happen, and “when” it happens is determined by where you place it. That’s also why you need context to read state: You need to use the current document position to know where on the state’s “thread” you are.

```typst
self.update( function any ) → content
```

- `update` — #lorem(5).split().map(list.item).join() — Required Positional
  - If given a non-function value, sets the state to that value.

#### Notes

However, be aware that integers larger than 263−1 or smaller than −263 will be converted to floating-point numbers, which may result in an approximative value. - Custom YAML tags are ignored, though the loaded value will still be present. - Bytes are not encoded as YAML sequences for performance and readability reasons. Consider using cbor.encode for binary data.

### 3.14.4 artifact Element

#### kind

The artifact kind. You can improve accessibility by using the most specific artifact kind available. Your choice will govern how the PDF reader treats the artifact during reflow and content extraction (e.g. copy and paste). Artifact types have been introduced in various different PDF specifications. Depending on which PDF version you target, Typst will select the most appropriate artifact type using your selection here.

  The path of the file to be attached. Must always be specified, but is only read from if no data is provided in the following argument.

  The relationship of the attached file to the document. Ignored if export doesn’t target PDF/A-3.
- `mime-type` — Settable; default: none
  The MIME type of the attached file. 4. attach
- `description` — Settable; default: none
  A description for the attached file.
